assignments.name: Semester Start Attestations
assignments.instructions:
Four short attestations. Read each one carefully and sign your name in the space provided. Credit is for completion.

This is not the Pulse Check. The Pulse Check is a separate, anonymous survey about your background. Please complete both.

assignments.name: Semester Start Pulse Check
assignments.instructions:
This survey tells me who is actually in the room, so I can pitch the course correctly. It takes about five minutes.

Read this before you answer:

Credit is for completing the survey. There are no right answers, and nothing here is scored on content.

Nothing you say here will ever be used in an academic integrity context or held against you in any way.

Please answer honestly, especially about AI. An accurate picture of how this class actually works helps me build a course worth your time. A flattering one does not.

assignments.name: Rhythm Portfolio · Week 01
assignments.instructions:
Portfolio Entry 0 — The number you signed

Covers class 1 (Thu 8/27). Canvas text entry. AI off — this is your judgment, not the agent's.

On Thursday a client asked: what is a fireplace worth in Eastville? An AI agent answered $52,776, and you were asked to sign off on that number before it went into the client memo.

Answer three things. Short is fine; a sentence each is the target.

What you signed. Paste the output of your signature cell exactly as it printed in class — name, Y or N, and your reason. Do not edit it. Signing "Y" is not penalized; most of the room did. What matters is that the record is honest.

What the $52,776 actually measured. In business English, no jargon: what was the agent really comparing when it compared homes with and without a fireplace?

What you would have needed to see to sign. Describe the evidence, table, or comparison that would have let you put your name on a fireplace number with confidence. You don't need to know how to produce it yet.

You will reopen this entry in Session 10 and rewrite line 3 with a number you computed yourself.

How the portfolio is graded — read this once, it applies every week: presence and seriousness, never correctness. A crossed-out wrong answer left visible scores higher than a suspiciously clean one. You are graded for doing the thinking, not for being right.

10 — complete and serious: all three lines answered in your own words, signature unedited

5 — present but token or partial

0 — missing

Light weeks (exam week, break weeks) are expected to be thin — submit what the sessions produced.

assignments.name: Item F · Adversary Check (Session 2 spec)
assignments.instructions:
The adversary check. Individual — one submission per student, even though the spec was written in pairs.

Photograph or retype your pair's spec (§1–6). Prompt an AI:

"Here is our data spec: [paste §1–6]. Attack it: what would make this comparison unfair? What data are we assuming exists that might not?"

Submit one page: the best attack it produced, and your fix — or why you're rejecting the attack. Include the prompt you used and the AI's response (a screenshot or paste is fine).

The rules: an AI may not write your spec. An AI must attack it. Disclosure is never penalized; non-disclosure is an integrity issue.

Upload a PDF or Word file, or paste your page in the text box. Goes in the portfolio.

assignments.name: Rhythm Portfolio · Week 02
assignments.instructions:
Rhythm Portfolio — Week 02: The file arrived

Three short entries. Business English, no code. AI is forbidden for this entry. Graded for presence and seriousness, not correctness.

Your §2, repaired. Rewrite the decision line of your spec so it names the decider — who acts on the basement number, doing what differently. (Thursday's discussion; check #3 on the Ask Card.) One or two sentences.

Ledger row s3, in your words. What was found, what was fixed, what is still unknown — and for whom. No code words. If your Thursday line said "the data was dirty," this is the rewrite.

The 111. Your two hypotheses for where three extra rows came from, and which one you would test first and how you would know. Describe the check in plain English; don't write it.

A specific wrong hypothesis scores full marks. A vague right one does not.

Type your answers here. No file upload.

assignments.name: Cycle 1 Groups
assignments.instructions:
Cycle 1 working groups

Random groups of 4 or 5, formed within your section. Used for every Cycle 1 group activity.

I will post your group members' names and emails in a comment on this assignment.

Once you see that comment:

Read the names and emails.

Reach out to your group so you can find each other.

Type Received (or a short note) in the text box below and submit.

This assignment is 5 points. The submission is how I know you have the information.

assignments.name: S4 homework — The missing age
assignments.instructions:
In class you made a first call on the 11 homes missing age, on one piece of evidence: they are about $39K cheaper than the other 97. Tonight you test that call against more evidence and commit to it.

Work in today's notebook. Start from this cell — it is Tuesday and Thursday's fixes in one place, so you do not need anything you saved in class:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv('eastville_teaching.csv')
df['price'] = df['price'].str.replace('$','',regex=False).str.replace(',','',regex=False).astype(int)
df = df.drop_duplicates()
len(df) # 108

Then reuse the comparison code from today. About 20 minutes.

AI: permitted, with disclosure. One line on anything AI helped with — what did you check before trusting it? Disclosure is never penalized; not disclosing is an integrity issue.

Graded on presence, not on which choice you made. Changing your mind since class is a good answer — say what changed it.

assignments.name: Team startup — one call, one ledger
assignments.instructions:
Objective

Your team now has one shared position: one set of decisions, one ledger. Five of you made the age call individually last week. At least one of you probably decided differently from the others. Reconciling that — in writing, with a number — is the work.

From here on, every Cycle 1 deliverable is built on the decisions and the ledger you produce today.

Instructions

1 · Agree on the spine. Put all five individual age decisions on the table. Decide as a team: keep all 108 homes, or drop to 97. Then, in two sentences, record the decision — one of them citing a specific number — and name who changed their mind and what changed it. "We all agreed" is a red flag, not an answer; if nobody moved, say why the evidence didn't move anyone.

2 · House 108. Four Eastville homes sell above $500,000. The largest is house 108 — $675,030, 3,222 sqft, Apple Valley. Report the mean price with and without it. Then decide: is house 108 part of "a typical Eastville home," or not? One line, and say what you would need to know to be sure. This is your second exclusion decision in a week. Notice that it has the same shape as the first one.

3 · Write the team ledger. Rows s2 through s5, merged from your five individual ledgers into one. One line per row, business English, your words. At the top, name the decider your team writes to for the rest of Cycle 1 — buyer, seller, or agent.

AI: permitted, with disclosure. One line on anything AI helped with: what did you check before trusting it?

What to submit

One submission per team. Paste into the text box, in this order:

Team number and all five names

The spine decision — two sentences, one number, and who changed their mind

House 108 — both means, your call, one line

Your decider, then the four ledger rows (s2, s3, s4, s5)

Your AI disclosure line, if any

Graded on presence, not on which way you decided. A team that switched positions and said why scores full marks.

assignments.name: S6 homework — Hold one thing equal
assignments.instructions:
In class the basement gap was $65,160 on the whole file. Held to 3-bedroom homes it was $35K; held to 4-bedroom homes, $99K — and one side of that comparison had three homes. Tonight you run the slices yourself and decide how small is too small.

Work in today's notebook. Start from this cell — Tuesday and Thursday's fixes in one place, so you do not need anything you saved in class:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv('eastville_teaching.csv')
df['price'] = df['price'].str.replace('$','',regex=False).str.replace(',','',regex=False).astype(int)
df = df.drop_duplicates()
len(df) # 108

Every slice below is the same two lines — a filter, then today's groupby. .agg(['mean', 'count']) gives the average and the number of homes in one call:
homes = df[df['beds'] == 3] # ← the slice
homes.groupby('basement')['price'].agg(['mean', 'count']).round(0)

About 20 minutes. Answers, not code.

AI: permitted, with disclosure. One line on anything AI helped with — what did you check before trusting it? Disclosure is never penalized; not disclosing is an integrity issue.

Graded on presence, not on which call you made. "Report the average of eight homes" is a legitimate answer if it says eight.

assignments.name: S7 homework — The fireplace, three ways
assignments.instructions:
Objective

In session 1 most of you signed the $53K fireplace gap, and the room could not say what was wrong with it. Session 6 gave you the way to find out — run the same groupby on everything else. Session 7 gave you the picture, and the sentence that goes under it. This week you do all three on the fireplace: the gap, the reasons, the chart.

Instructions

Work in the session 7 notebook. Start from this cell — sessions 3 and 4's fixes plus session 7's price_chart, so you do not need anything you saved in class:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv('eastville_teaching.csv')
df['price'] = df['price'].str.replace('$','',regex=False).str.replace(',','',regex=False).astype(int)
df = df.drop_duplicates()

def price_chart(by):
 means = df.groupby(by)['price'].mean()
 means.plot.bar(title=f"Average price by {by}")
 return means

Three questions, about 20 minutes in total. Answers, not code. Report numbers you computed — not ones shown in class.

AI policy

Permitted, with disclosure. One line on anything AI helped with — what did you check before trusting it? Disclosure is never penalized; not disclosing is an integrity issue.

Grading

Graded on presence, not on which chart or which caption you chose. A caption that names a specific number the chart hides is a good caption whichever chart it sits under.

assignments.name: S8 homework — Whose homes is the line standing on?
assignments.instructions:
Objective

In class the line stood on all 108 homes and said $143 a square foot. Tonight you take homes away from it — first one, then eleven — and see whether the sentence survives. Both are session 4's question back again: whose homes is the number standing on?

Instructions

Work in the session 8 notebook. Start from this cell — sessions 3 and 4's fixes plus today's line, so you do not need anything you saved in class:
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm

df = pd.read_csv('eastville_teaching.csv')
df['price'] = df['price'].str.replace('$','',regex=False).str.replace(',','',regex=False).astype(int)
df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=['house'])

y = df['price']
X = sm.add_constant(df[['sqft']])
line = sm.OLS(y, X).fit()
line.params # const 56,487 · sqft 142.8 — the numbers you are NOT allowed to report

Two questions, about 20 minutes in total. Answers, not code. Report numbers you computed — $142.8 and $71,424 are barred.

AI policy

Permitted, with disclosure. One line on anything AI helped with — what did you check before trusting it? Disclosure is never penalized; not disclosing is an integrity issue.

Grading

Graded on presence, not on which call you made. "The sentence did not change" is a legitimate answer if it says by how much the number did.

assignments.name: Team ledger, part 2 — the basement, held fixed
assignments.instructions:
Objective

On Thursday the agent's model put the basement at $17,765. Tuesday's model, with size alone held fixed, put it at $50,701. Same homes, same basement, two numbers. Your team's job is to find out what moved it, decide what the memo can say about the basement, and bring your ledger up to date.

From here on, the ledger is the draft of your Cycle 1 memo.

Instructions

1 · Five models, one basement. Start from the s9 notebook's sqft + basement model and use d (the frame with the 0/1 style columns). Assign one change to each member, by name. Each member makes their change on their own laptop and reports the basement number and its interval:

add av

add style_Ranch and style_Two-story

add garage

add fire

take the agent's full column list and remove garage

Keep the three named lines — y = ..., X = ..., sm.OLS(y, X).fit() — and change only the column list.

2 · Line them up. Put your five numbers in order, between $50,701 (two columns) and $17,765 (all ten). Which change moved the basement most? Then run one groupby that shows why: what do basement homes have more of? Hint: the mean of a 0/1 column is a share.

3 · The agent's line. The agent wrote: "The basement fell from $50,701 to $17,765 once we held the house fixed — it lost two-thirds of its value." Sign it or don't, in one team sentence that uses your answer to step 2.

4 · Update the team ledger. Rows s6, s7, s8 and s9, merged from your five individual ledgers into one. One line per row, business English, your words. The s9 row must cite an interval, not just a point. Name who drafted s9 and what the team changed in it. If nobody changed anything, say why the draft already held.

AI policy

AI: permitted, with disclosure. One line on anything AI helped with: what did you check before trusting it?

What to submit

One submission per team. Paste into the text box, in this order:

Team number and all five names

Step 1 — for each member: name, their change, the basement number and its interval

Step 2 — the five in order, the change that moved it most, your groupby line and what it showed

Step 3 — your sentence

The four ledger rows (s6, s7, s8, s9), then who drafted s9 and what changed

Your AI disclosure line, if any

Grading

Graded on presence, not on which way you decided. Each member's step-1 number must be one they computed. A team that disagreed and said how it resolved it scores full marks.

assignments.name: S10 homework — The school zone, four ways
assignments.instructions:
Objective

In class the basement moved from $18K to $30K across four defensible models, and three of the four could not tell it from zero. Tonight you do the same reading for Apple Valley and decide whether it is a number you sign or a range you report.

Instructions

Work in the session 10 notebook. Run §1 (setup) and the four models under STOP 2 — you do not need anything you saved in class. Read the av row — coefficient and both interval columns — off each of A, B, C and D.

About 20 minutes. Answers, not code. Report numbers you computed — the basement numbers are barred.

AI policy

Permitted, with disclosure. One line on anything AI helped with — what did you check before trusting it? Disclosure is never penalized; not disclosing is an integrity issue.

Grading

Graded on presence, not on which model you defend. "Fragile, and here is the range" is a full-marks answer if the range is yours and the reason names the data.

announcements.title: Class 12: Are online customers more profitable?
announcements.body:
Class 12: Are online customers more profitable?

Today you audited an AI agent's work on a bank's customer file, alone and with no AI: eight claims across three stages, sign or don't sign. The first two stages came down to asking who was removed before trusting what is left, and to a $5 gap that hid a real difference inside each age group. Some claims were fine, and signing those counted too. Stage C stays sealed.

Next class (Thu 10/8): your team settles Stage C before anyone sees the answers. Then the memo, finished at your table. Exam 1 is Thu 10/15.

announcements.title: Paid fellowship — help redesign ISOM 352 for the AI era
announcements.body:
Paid fellowship — help redesign ISOM 352 for the AI era

ISOM 352 is being rebuilt around one question: when an AI agent can run the Python → pandas → regression stack for you, what's left for a human to be good at? My answer is specification and audit literacy — framing a problem precisely, and knowing when the agent's answer is wrong.

I'm looking for one BBA student to co-design and pilot the new materials as a Robson Fellow — a paid role (stipend funded by the Robson Innovation in Research and Teaching Grant). You'd help build agent-based exercises where the AI deliberately produces plausible-but-wrong output and students learn to catch it.

You're a fit if you're comfortable in Python, use AI tools heavily (especially if you've hit that "the agent gave me an answer and I'm not sure it's right" feeling), and want to reshape how business education works in an AI world. Any background is welcome — you just need to be a BBA student.

To apply (short is fine), email wenjun.gu@emory.edu (mailto:wenjun.gu@emory.edu) with the subject line "Robson Fellow application":

Name, program, year

2–3 sentences on why this interests you

A line on your Python comfort and how you actually use AI in your work

Resume/CV (required)

Deadline: end of day Tuesday, September 29. I have to name the Fellow in a grant packet this week, so I can't consider late entries.

announcements.title: Class 9: Which premium survives?
announcements.body:
Class 9: Which premium survives?
Today you held the house fixed and watched the premiums collapse. The fireplace's $52K became $8K and vanished. The basement's $65K shrank to $18K — but its interval still touched $0, so you couldn't sign it. Only Apple Valley survived, at $27K. A number has a give-or-take, and the give-or-take is what you sign.
Next class (Tue 9/29): five models, one basement — does its fate depend on the model?

announcements.title: Class 7: Which picture is telling the truth?
announcements.body:
Class 7: Which picture is telling the truth?
Today the agent drew the buyer's “which zone” answer, then “tidied” one chart by starting its axis at $280,000 instead of $0 — small gaps looked enormous. You refused the captions that didn't survive the check, fixed the chart in as few lines as you could, and chose bar or box for the memo. Keep the two words that start every honest answer: it depends — mean or median? On the skewness. Mild or heavy? Each “depends” is a step, not a stall.

announcements.title: Class 6: Is it the basement, or is it the house?
announcements.body:
Today you ran the basement's number the way the agent ran the fireplace's — same groupby, and it came back $65,160 more for basement homes on the mean. Then the one-line check that would have caught day one: run the groupby on everything else. The homes aren't otherwise-similar — 3.7 vs 3.3 bedrooms, 2.7 vs 2.4 baths, twice as likely in Apple Valley. You sign "sell for more," not "adds" — the $65K is the basement and everything that comes with it.

Next class (Thu 9/17): the picture version — what does a chart catch that the table hides?

announcements.title: Class 5: What is a typical Eastville home worth?
announcements.body:
Today you wrote the first sentence of a memo and found the hard part is the word, not the number. Price's mean ($341,395) sits $9,680 above the median — four homes over $500K drag it up — while square footage has no tail, so its mean and median agree. Same statistic, honest once and misleading once. For categories, "most common" names the biggest group — "most" claims more than half, so check the share first. Look before you choose.

Next class (Tue 9/15): two variables — what moves with what?

announcements.title: Welcome to ISOM 352 ADA
announcements.body:
Hello and welcome to ISOM 352 Applied Data Analytics with Coding (ADA)!

I hope you had a great summer break. My name is Prof. Wen Gu, an Associate Professor in the ISOM area of Goizueta. As we start the new term, I'm excited to dive into the world of coding with all of you and explore the world of data and its role in business decision-making. This course will cover a wide range of topics, including Python programming, data visualization and analytics, querying data with SQL, and an introduction to machine learning and artificial intelligence. We will also discuss how to implement analytics and how to effectively communicate findings.

Our first class meeting is on Thursday 8/27 in Goizueta Room W330 (West Wing).
